q: How many questions are there in the Life in the UK test?
a: 24 questions
s: 24 questions

q: What are the test questions based on?
a: ALL parts of the handbook
d: Only the summary of key facts
s: ALL parts of the handbook

q: What level of English do the Life in the UK test questions require?
a: ESOL Entry Level 3
s: ESOL Entry Level 3

q: From October 2013, what English evidence is needed for settlement alongside the test?
a: Speaking and listening skills at B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference
d: Speaking and listening skills at A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference
C1 of the Common European Framework
s: Speaking and listening skills at B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference

q: Name the five fundamental principles of British life.
a: Democracy; the rule of law; individual liberty; tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs; participation in community life
d: Democracy; monarchy; free trade; low taxes; strong armed forces
Democracy; socialism; individual liberty; religious unity; patriotism
s: Democracy; the rule of law; individual liberty; tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs; participation in community life

q: In the citizenship pledge, new citizens promise to give their loyalty to what?
a: The United Kingdom, and respect its rights and freedoms
d: The King personally, and his heirs
s: The United Kingdom

q: According to the handbook, what has no place in British society?
a: Extremism or intolerance
s: Extremism or intolerance

q: Which of these is a responsibility you should respect as a permanent resident or citizen?
a: Look after the area in which you live and the environment
s: Look after the area in which you live and the environment

q: Which of these freedoms does the UK offer in return for its residents' responsibilities?
a: A right to a fair trial
s: A right to a fair trial

q: Who normally must pass the Life in the UK test to become permanent residents?
a: People here on work visas, including those on Tier 1 and Tier 2 of the points-based system
d: Only people from outside Europe, because EU citizens are exempt from the Life in the UK test for settlement
s: People here on work visas, including those on Tier 1 and Tier 2 of the points-based system

q: What should you do if your standard of English is below ESOL Entry Level 3?
a: Pass an ESOL course in English with Citizenship, with a test at the end
d: Take the test in your own language
s: Pass an ESOL course in English with Citizenship, with a test at the end

q: Which countries make up the UK?
a: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
s: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland

q: What is the official name of the country?
a: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
d: The United Kingdom of Britain and Ireland
s: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

q: What does 'Great Britain' refer to?
a: Only England, Scotland and Wales, not Northern Ireland
d: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
The whole of the British Isles including Ireland
s: Only England, Scotland and Wales, not Northern Ireland

q: What are the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man called?
a: Crown dependencies — closely linked with the UK but not part of it
s: Crown dependencies

q: St Helena and the Falkland Islands are examples of what?
a: British overseas territories linked to the UK but not part of it
s: British overseas territories

q: What is the status of the rest of Ireland (outside Northern Ireland)?
a: An independent country
s: An independent country

q: Where does the parliament that governs the UK sit?
a: Westminster
s: Westminster

q: What do Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have?
a: Parliaments or assemblies of their own, with devolved powers in defined areas
d: No governing bodies of their own
s: Parliaments or assemblies of their own, with devolved powers in defined areas

q: What were the first people to live in Britain?
a: Hunter-gatherers, in what we call the Stone Age
s: Hunter-gatherers

q: When did Britain become permanently separated from the continent by the Channel?
a: About 10,000 years ago
s: About 10,000 years ago

q: What is Stonehenge and where is it?
a: A Stone Age monument in the English county of Wiltshire
d: A Bronze Age village in Wales
A Viking burial site in Yorkshire
s: A Stone Age monument in the English county of Wiltshire

q: What is Skara Brae?
a: The best preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe, on Orkney, off the north coast of Scotland
d: The best preserved Roman town in northern Europe, on the south coast of England near Dover
s: The best preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe, on Orkney, off the north coast of Scotland

q: How did people live in the Bronze Age?
a: In roundhouses, and they buried their dead in tombs called round barrows
s: In roundhouses

q: What language did people speak in the Iron Age?
a: A language from the Celtic language family
d: An early form of Anglo-Saxon brought over by settlers from northern Europe
s: A language from the Celtic language family

q: What happened for the first time in the Iron Age in Britain?
a: The people made the first coins to be minted in Britain, some inscribed with the names of Iron Age kings
d: The first paved roads were built, linking the hill forts to the coastal trading settlements
s: The people made the first coins to be minted in Britain, some inscribed with the names of Iron Age kings

q: Who led a Roman invasion of Britain in 55 BC that was unsuccessful?
a: Julius Caesar
s: Julius Caesar

q: When did the Romans successfully invade Britain, and under which emperor?
a: In AD 43, under the Emperor Claudius
s: In AD 43, under the Emperor Claudius

q: Who was Boudicca?
a: A queen of the Iceni tribe who fought against the Romans; there is a statue of her on Westminster Bridge in London
d: A Saxon queen who fought against the Vikings; her statue stands at the entrance to the Tower of London
The first Christian queen of Britain
s: A queen of the Iceni tribe who fought against the Romans; there is a statue of her on Westminster Bridge in London

q: Why was Hadrian's Wall built?
a: On the orders of the Roman Emperor Hadrian, to keep out the Picts (ancestors of the Scottish people)
d: To mark the border with Wales
s: On the orders of the Roman Emperor Hadrian

q: Which forts on Hadrian's Wall can still be visited?
a: Housesteads and Vindolanda
s: Housesteads and Vindolanda

q: How long did the Romans remain in Britain?
a: 400 years (they ruled from AD 43 to 410)
s: 400 years

q: When did the first Christian communities begin to appear in Britain?
a: During the 3rd and 4th centuries AD
s: During the 3rd and 4th centuries AD

q: Which tribes invaded Britain after the Romans left?
a: The Jutes, the Angles and the Saxons, from northern Europe
d: The Picts, the Gauls and the Franks
s: The Jutes, the Angles and the Saxons, from northern Europe

q: By about which year were Anglo-Saxon kingdoms established in Britain?
a: By about AD 600
s: By about AD 600

q: What was found at Sutton Hoo in Suffolk?
a: The burial place of one of the Anglo-Saxon kings, buried with treasure and armour in a ship covered by a mound of earth
d: A Viking longship, buried with weapons and treasure, that carried raiders up the rivers of East Anglia
s: The burial place of one of the Anglo-Saxon kings, buried with treasure and armour in a ship covered by a mound of earth

q: Who were St Columba and St Augustine?
a: Missionaries who came to Britain to preach about Christianity — Columba in what is now Scotland, Augustine in the south of England
d: Viking leaders who converted to Christianity
s: Missionaries who came to Britain to preach about Christianity

q: St Augustine became the first Archbishop of where?
a: Canterbury
s: Canterbury

q: Where did the Vikings come from?
a: Denmark and Norway
s: Denmark and Norway

q: When did the Vikings first visit Britain?
a: In AD 789, to raid coastal towns and take away goods and slaves
s: In AD 789

q: Which king defeated the Vikings and united the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms of England?
a: King Alfred the Great
s: King Alfred the Great

q: What is the area of the east and north of England where Viking languages and customs dominated called?
a: The Danelaw — many place names there, such as Grimsby and Scunthorpe, come from the Viking languages
s: The Danelaw

q: Who united the tribes in the north of what is now Scotland against Viking attack?
a: Kenneth MacAlpin — the term Scotland began to be used to describe that country
s: Kenneth MacAlpin

q: What happened at the Battle of Hastings in 1066?
a: William, the Duke of Normandy, defeated Harold, the Saxon king of England; Harold was killed in the battle
d: The Vikings under King Canute defeated the Anglo-Saxons, and Harold fled into exile in Normandy
s: William, the Duke of Normandy, defeated Harold, the Saxon king of England; Harold was killed in the battle

q: What is the Bayeux Tapestry?
a: An embroidery, still displayed in France today, that commemorates the Battle of Hastings
d: A Norman law book, still kept in France today, recording the laws William introduced after the Conquest
s: An embroidery, still displayed in France today, that commemorates the Battle of Hastings

q: What was the Domesday Book?
a: A list William the Conqueror had made of all the towns and villages, showing who owned the land and what animals they owned
d: A history of the Norman kings, written by monks to record the deeds of William the Conqueror and his sons
s: A list William the Conqueror had made of all the towns and villages, showing who owned the land and what animals they owned

q: What was the last successful foreign invasion of England?
a: The Norman Conquest in 1066
s: The Norman Conquest in 1066

q: What period do we call the Middle Ages?
a: The period from the Norman Conquest (1066) up until about 1485 — a period of almost constant war
d: The period from the Roman invasion (AD 43) up until the Norman Conquest of 1066
s: The period from the Norman Conquest (1066) up until about 1485

q: What were the Crusades?
a: Wars in which European Christians fought for control of the Holy Land
s: Wars in which European Christians fought for control of the Holy Land

q: What happened at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314?
a: The Scottish king Robert the Bruce defeated the English, and Scotland remained unconquered by the English
s: The Scottish king Robert the Bruce defeated the English

q: What did the Statute of Rhuddlan do in 1284?
a: It annexed Wales to the Crown of England, under King Edward I
d: It created the first English Parliament
s: It annexed Wales to the Crown of England, under King Edward I

q: What did the English kings build in Wales to maintain their power?
a: Huge castles, including Conwy and Caernarvon, many of which still stand today
d: A great stone wall along the border with England, long stretches of which can still be visited today
s: Huge castles, including Conwy and Caernarvon, many of which still stand today

q: By which year were the last Welsh rebellions defeated?
a: By 1415, and English laws and the English language were then introduced in Wales

q: What was 'the Pale' in Ireland?
a: The area around Dublin ruled by the English — elsewhere Irish chieftains and lords ruled
d: A wall built to keep out the Irish
An area ruled by the Vikings
s: The area around Dublin ruled by the English

q: What was the Hundred Years War?
a: A long period of war between England and France that actually lasted 116 years
d: A war between England and Scotland
A war between England and Spain
s: A long period of war between England and France that actually lasted 116 years

q: What happened at the Battle of Agincourt in 1415?
a: King Henry V's vastly outnumbered English army defeated the French
s: King Henry V's vastly outnumbered English army defeated the French

q: When did the English leave France?
a: In the 1450s
s: In the 1450s

q: What was the Black Death and when did it come to Britain?
a: A form of plague that came to Britain in 1348 and killed over one third of the population of England, Wales and Scotland
d: A famine in 1348 that killed one tenth of the population
A plague in 1665 that killed half of London
s: A form of plague that came to Britain in 1348 and killed over one third of the population of England, Wales and Scotland

q: What social changes followed the Black Death?
a: Labour shortages led to higher wages, people moved into towns, and new social classes appeared, including owners of large areas of land (later called the gentry) and a strong middle class
d: Wages fell and towns emptied permanently
s: Labour shortages led to higher wages, people moved into towns

q: What was Magna Carta and when was it signed?
a: A charter of rights agreed by King John in 1215 — it limited the power of the king and protected the rights of the nobility
d: A law of 1215 that gave all men the vote
A peace treaty with France in 1415
s: A charter of rights agreed by King John in 1215

q: What did Parliament develop into in England during the Middle Ages?
a: Two Houses: the House of Lords (nobility, great landowners and bishops) and the House of Commons (knights and wealthy people from towns and cities)
d: A single council of church leaders and royal judges that advised the king on taxes but could not pass laws
An assembly elected by all adults
s: Two Houses: the House of Lords (nobility, great landowners and bishops) and the House of Commons (knights and wealthy people from towns and cities)

q: In Scotland, how many Houses did Parliament have in the Middle Ages?
a: Three Houses, called Estates: the lords, the commons and the clergy
s: Three Houses, called Estates

q: By about 1400, what language was preferred in the royal courts and official documents in England?
a: English — a combination of Norman French and Anglo-Saxon
s: English

q: Who wrote The Canterbury Tales?
a: Geoffrey Chaucer — a series of poems about people travelling to Canterbury on a pilgrimage
s: Geoffrey Chaucer

q: Who was the first person in England to print books using a printing press?
a: William Caxton — The Canterbury Tales was one of the first books he printed
s: William Caxton

q: What were the Wars of the Roses?
a: A civil war begun in 1455 to decide who should be king of England, fought between the House of Lancaster (red rose) and the House of York (white rose)
d: A series of wars between England and France, begun in 1455, over who should inherit the French crown
A rebellion of peasants against the king
s: A civil war begun in 1455 to decide who should be king of England, fought between the House of Lancaster (red rose) and the House of York (white rose)

q: How did the Wars of the Roses end?
a: At the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485: King Richard III of the House of York was killed and Henry Tudor became King Henry VII
d: At the Battle of Agincourt in 1415
With the signing of Magna Carta
s: At the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485

q: What symbol did the House of Tudor adopt?
a: A red rose with a white rose inside it, as a sign that the Houses of York and Lancaster were now allies
s: A red rose with a white rose inside it

q: What is Henry VIII most famous for?
a: Breaking away from the Church of Rome and marrying six times
s: Breaking away from the Church of Rome and marrying six times

q: Who was Henry VIII's first wife and what happened to her?
a: Catherine of Aragon, a Spanish princess — Henry divorced her when she was too old to give him another child; their surviving child was Mary
d: Jane Seymour — she died after childbirth
s: Catherine of Aragon, a Spanish princess

q: What happened to Anne Boleyn?
a: She was accused of taking lovers and executed at the Tower of London; she and Henry had one daughter, Elizabeth
d: She died shortly after giving birth to the son Henry wanted, and was buried at Westminster Abbey
Henry divorced her for political reasons
She survived Henry and married again
s: She was accused of taking lovers and executed at the Tower of London; she and Henry had one daughter, Elizabeth

q: Which wife gave Henry VIII the son he wanted?
a: Jane Seymour — the son was Edward, but Jane died shortly after the birth
s: Jane Seymour

q: Why did Henry VIII establish the Church of England?
a: The Pope refused to approve his divorce from Catherine of Aragon, so Henry created a Church where the king, not the Pope, had power to appoint bishops and order how people should worship
d: He wanted to become a Protestant reformer
The Pope excommunicated the whole of England first
s: The Pope refused to approve his divorce from Catherine of Aragon

q: What was the Reformation?
a: A movement against the authority of the Pope and the ideas and practices of the Roman Catholic Church, which formed Protestant ideas across Europe
d: A movement to reform Parliament and extend the vote to ordinary people across Protestant Europe
The reform of the voting system
s: A movement against the authority of the Pope and the ideas and practices of the Roman Catholic Church

q: During whose reign was Wales formally united with England?
a: Henry VIII's — by the Act for the Government of Wales; Welsh representatives were sent to the House of Commons
s: Henry VIII's

q: What is Edward VI remembered for?
a: The Book of Common Prayer, written during his reign for the Church of England; he was strongly Protestant and died at 15
d: Restoring the Catholic religion in England and ordering a new Latin prayer book for every parish church
s: The Book of Common Prayer, written during his reign for the Church of England; he was strongly Protestant and died at 15

q: Why was Queen Mary known as 'Bloody Mary'?
a: She was a devout Catholic who persecuted Protestants for their religious beliefs
d: She led England into a bloody war with France
She suppressed a rebellion in Ireland
s: She was a devout Catholic who persecuted Protestants for their religious beliefs

q: Who became queen after Mary's death?
a: Her half-sister Elizabeth, daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn
s: Her half-sister Elizabeth

q: What happened to the Spanish Armada in 1588?
a: Elizabeth I's English fleet defeated the large Spanish fleet sent to conquer England and restore Catholicism
d: It was destroyed by the French navy before it could reach England, ending Spain's war with France
s: Elizabeth I's English fleet defeated the large Spanish fleet sent to conquer England and restore Catholicism

q: Who was Mary, Queen of Scots?
a: The Catholic queen of Scotland — she fled to England, was held prisoner by Elizabeth I for 20 years, and was executed for plotting against Elizabeth
s: The Catholic queen of Scotland

q: What was the Elizabethan period known for?
a: A growing sense of English patriotism, expanded trade, and rich poetry and drama
s: A growing sense of English patriotism, expanded trade

q: Who was Sir Francis Drake?
a: One of the commanders in the defeat of the Spanish Armada and one of the founders of England's naval tradition; his ship, the Golden Hind, was one of the first to sail right around the world
d: The founder of the Royal Society and the first Englishman to map the coasts of the New World for Queen Elizabeth I
s: One of the commanders in the defeat of the Spanish Armada and one of the founders of England's naval tradition; his ship, the Golden Hind, was one of the first to sail right around the world

q: Where was William Shakespeare born?
a: In Stratford-upon-Avon, in 1564
s: In Stratford-upon-Avon, in 1564

q: Which of these lines was coined by Shakespeare?
a: 'To be or not to be' — from Hamlet
d: 'Do not go gentle into that good night'
s: 'To be or not to be'

q: Who became King of England when Elizabeth I died in 1603?
a: Her cousin James VI of Scotland, who became King James I of England, Wales and Ireland — Elizabeth never married and had no children
s: Her cousin James VI of Scotland

q: What is the King James Bible?
a: A new translation of the Bible into English, also known as the Authorised Version, produced during James I's reign
d: The first Bible printed in Latin
A Catholic prayer book in Latin, ordered by James I for use in the churches of England and Scotland
A history of the kings of England
s: A new translation of the Bible into English, also known as the Authorised Version, produced during James I's reign

q: What were the Plantations in Ireland under Elizabeth I and James I?
a: The English government took land from Catholic landholders and gave it to Protestant settlers from England and Scotland, especially in Ulster
d: Farms set up to grow potatoes
New towns built by the government to house Irish workers who had lost their farmland in the famine
s: The English government took land from Catholic landholders and gave it to Protestant settlers from England and Scotland, especially in Ulster

q: What did Charles I believe about the monarchy?
a: In the 'Divine Right of Kings' — that kings were directly appointed by God to rule
d: That Parliament should control the king
That the Church should choose kings
s: In the 'Divine Right of Kings'

q: Why did war break out between Charles I and Scotland?
a: Charles introduced a revised Prayer Book and tried to impose it on the Presbyterian Church in Scotland, causing serious unrest
d: The Scottish Parliament refused to pay taxes for the king's wars and expelled his bishops from Edinburgh
s: Charles introduced a revised Prayer Book and tried to impose it on the Presbyterian Church in Scotland, causing serious unrest

q: What were the two sides in the English Civil War called?
a: The king's supporters were the Cavaliers, and Parliament's supporters were the Roundheads
s: The king's supporters were the Cavaliers

q: At which battles was the king's army defeated in the Civil War?
a: The Battles of Marston Moor and Naseby
s: The Battles of Marston Moor and Naseby

q: What happened to Charles I?
a: He was executed in 1649, and England declared itself a republic called the Commonwealth
d: He escaped to France and died in exile
He abdicated in favour of his son
s: He was executed in 1649

q: What title was Oliver Cromwell given?
a: Lord Protector — he led England until his death, while Britain was without a king
s: Lord Protector

q: After which battles was Charles II defeated before escaping to Europe?
a: The Battles of Dunbar and Worcester — he famously hid in an oak tree on one occasion
s: The Battles of Dunbar and Worcester

q: What was the Restoration?
a: In May 1660, Parliament invited Charles II to come back from exile in the Netherlands and he was crowned king — the monarchy was restored
d: The rebuilding of London after the Great Fire
The return of the Catholic Church to England in May 1660, after the death of Oliver Cromwell
s: In May 1660, Parliament invited Charles II to come back from exile in the Netherlands and he was crowned king

q: What did the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679 guarantee?
a: That no one could be held prisoner unlawfully — every prisoner has a right to a court hearing
s: That no one could be held prisoner unlawfully

q: What happened in London in 1665?
a: The Great Plague — a major outbreak of plague; thousands died, especially in poorer areas
s: The Great Plague

q: What followed the Great Fire of London in 1666?
a: Much of the city was destroyed and had to be rebuilt; St Paul's Cathedral was designed and built by Sir Christopher Wren
d: The plague spread further through the ruined city, and the royal court moved to Oxford for a decade
The king moved the capital to York
London was abandoned for a decade
s: Much of the city was destroyed and had to be rebuilt; St Paul's Cathedral was designed and built by Sir Christopher Wren

q: What was the Royal Society?
a: Formed under Charles II, it is the oldest surviving scientific society in the world; early members included Sir Edmund Halley and Sir Isaac Newton
d: The king's private council of advisers, set up under Charles II to direct scientific and religious policy in England
s: Formed under Charles II, it is the oldest surviving scientific society in the world; early members included Sir Edmund Halley and Sir Isaac Newton

q: Why were many people alarmed when James II became king?
a: He was a Roman Catholic who favoured Catholics, acted against Protestant clergy and ignored Parliament — and his new son would be brought up Catholic
d: He was too young to rule
He wanted to abolish the monarchy and hand power to a council of Puritan clergy and army officers
s: He was a Roman Catholic who favoured Catholics, acted against Protestant clergy and ignored Parliament

q: What was the Glorious Revolution of 1688?
a: Important Protestants asked William of Orange, husband of James II's daughter Mary, to invade and proclaim himself king; there was no fighting in England and the revolution guaranteed the power of Parliament
d: A violent civil war that restored the Catholic Church
s: Important Protestants asked William of Orange, husband of James II's daughter Mary

q: What did the Bill of Rights of 1689 confirm?
a: The rights of Parliament and the limits of the king's power — the king could no longer raise taxes or administer justice without agreement from Parliament
d: The right of every man to vote
s: The rights of Parliament and the limits of the king's power

q: What is a constitutional monarchy?
a: A system in which the king or queen remains head of state but a constitution limits royal power — this developed in Britain after the Glorious Revolution
d: A monarchy in which the king or queen holds absolute power granted directly by a written constitution
A republic with an elected president
s: A system in which the king or queen remains head of state but a constitution limits royal power

q: Why could the monarch no longer rule alone after 1689?
a: The monarch needed Parliament's agreement — Parliament had to be called every year because the king needed money for wars and taxes could not be raised without it
d: The monarch was banned from London
s: The monarch needed Parliament's agreement

q: What was the Act of Union of 1707?
a: It united the kingdoms of England and Scotland and created the Kingdom of Great Britain; Scotland kept its own legal and education systems and Presbyterian Church
d: It united Great Britain and Ireland into a single kingdom and abolished Scotland's separate legal system and Church
s: It united the kingdoms of England and Scotland and created the Kingdom of Great Britain; Scotland kept its own legal and education systems and Presbyterian Church

q: Why did Sir Robert Walpole become the first Prime Minister?
a: King George I, a German, spoke poor English and relied heavily on his ministers — Walpole was Prime Minister from 1721 to 1742
d: George I died without an heir
He led a rebellion against the king
s: King George I, a German, spoke poor English and relied heavily on his ministers

q: What happened at the Battle of Culloden in 1746?
a: Charles Edward Stuart (Bonnie Prince Charlie), who had raised an army of Scottish clansmen to claim the throne, was defeated by George II's army; he escaped to Europe
s: Charles Edward Stuart (Bonnie Prince Charlie)

q: What were the Highland Clearances?
a: Scottish landlords destroyed small farms (crofts) to make room for large flocks of sheep and cattle; many Scottish people left for North America
d: The clearing of forests for farmland
The eviction of English settlers from the Scottish Highlands after the defeat of Bonnie Prince Charlie
A programme to build new Highland towns
s: Scottish landlords destroyed small farms (crofts) to make room for large flocks of sheep and cattle; many Scottish people left for North America

q: Who was Robert Burns?
a: A Scottish poet known as 'The Bard' — his best known work is Auld Lang Syne, sung at New Year (Hogmanay in Scotland)
d: A Welsh poet who wrote Under Milk Wood
The inventor of the steam engine
s: A Scottish poet known as 'The Bard'

q: What was the Enlightenment?
a: A period in the 18th century when new ideas about politics, philosophy and science developed — Adam Smith developed ideas about economics and David Hume about human nature
d: A religious revival movement of the 18th century, led by travelling preachers in Scotland and Wales
A period of censorship and control
s: A period in the 18th century when new ideas about politics, philosophy and science developed

q: Which important principle from the Enlightenment is still central today?
a: That everyone should have the right to their own political and religious beliefs and that the state should not try to dictate them
d: That the state should choose people's religion
That only landowners and church members should be free to hold political and religious opinions
That kings rule by divine right
s: That everyone should have the right to their own political and religious beliefs and that the state should not try to dictate them

q: Why is the Industrial Revolution significant for Britain?
a: Britain was the first country to industrialise on a large scale — machinery and steam power developed, and Britain produced more than half of the world's supplies of iron, coal and cotton cloth
d: Britain was the last country to industrialise
It made Britain mainly an agricultural country
s: Britain was the first country to industrialise on a large scale

q: Who was Richard Arkwright?
a: An Industrial Revolution figure remembered for efficiently and profitably running factories — he improved carding machines and used water power to drive machinery
d: A canal engineer who built the waterways carrying coal and cotton between the new industrial cities
The inventor of the jet engine
s: An Industrial Revolution figure remembered for efficiently and profitably running factories

q: Who was Sake Dean Mahomet?
a: He opened the Hindoostane Coffee House in London in 1810, the first curry house in Britain, and introduced 'shampooing' — the Indian art of head massage — to Britain
d: The first Indian member of Parliament, elected in London in 1810, who introduced curry houses to Britain
The founder of the East India Company
s: He opened the Hindoostane Coffee House in London in 1810, the first curry house in Britain

q: Who were the first formal anti-slavery groups set up by?
a: The Quakers, in the late 1700s
s: The Quakers, in the late 1700s

q: Who was William Wilberforce?
a: An evangelical Christian and MP who played an important part in changing the law — a leading abolitionist
d: A factory owner who campaigned in Parliament for shorter working hours for women and children
The founder of the Royal Navy
s: An evangelical Christian and MP who played an important part in changing the law

q: When did it become illegal to trade slaves in British ships or from British ports?
What did the Emancipation Act of 1833 do?
a: It abolished slavery throughout the British Empire
d: It banned the trading of slaves in British ships
s: It abolished slavery throughout the British Empire

q: After slavery was abolished, where did replacement workers come from?
a: Two million migrants came from India and China to replace the freed slaves
d: One million migrants came from Africa
s: Two million migrants came from India and China to replace the freed slaves

q: When did the American colonies declare independence?
a: In 1776, over taxation — Britain recognised the colonies' independence in 1783

q: What happened at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805?
a: Admiral Nelson defeated the combined French and Spanish fleets; Nelson was killed — Nelson's Column in Trafalgar Square commemorates him, and his ship HMS Victory can be visited in Portsmouth
d: The Duke of Wellington defeated Napoleon's combined fleet; Wellington was killed during the battle
s: Admiral Nelson defeated the combined French and Spanish fleets; Nelson was killed

q: How did the Napoleonic Wars end?
a: In 1815 the French Wars ended with the defeat of Napoleon by the Duke of Wellington at the Battle of Waterloo
d: With the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805
With a peace treaty signed in Paris in 1820, after Napoleon had defeated Wellington at Waterloo
With the French invasion of Britain
s: In 1815 the French Wars ended with the defeat of Napoleon by the Duke of Wellington at the Battle of Waterloo

q: Which crosses make up the Union Flag?
a: The cross of St George (England), the cross of St Andrew (Scotland) and the cross of St Patrick (Ireland)
d: The crosses of St George, St David and St Andrew
The crosses of St George, St Patrick and St David
The crosses of St Andrew, St Columba and St George
